name: PT Jasa Marga (Persero) Tbk

frontmatter.title: Jasa Marga: the build tail ends before the price does
frontmatter.summary: Indonesia's dominant toll operator trades at a stressed multiple near the bottom of its range. The zero-margin construction pass-through is shrinking, the current build programme is closing and the concession runway is long. We initiate at BUY: on a conservative maintenance-capex definition the AFFO yield already clears the ten-year sovereign, and the price refuses to pay for the post-build cash.
thesis: The zero-margin construction pass-through that carried the capex peak is contracting, so consolidated margins and cash conversion improve without any assumption of higher toll tariffs.
The current Trans-Java build programme is closing; the last section opened in October and the next large project carries its own syndicated facility, so group capex normalises from the peak.
Tariffs are a mechanical biennial reset on lagged inflation and service standards, and the sections now entering their cycle give a scheduled, non-discretionary revenue uplift.
Leverage is high but laddered and long-dated, with interest cover consistent with the disclosed ratio and no refinancing wall in the forecast period.

Both prior trade theses on this name were killed on the AFFO-versus-sovereign gate at the peak of the build. Computed rather than assumed, AFFO clears the sovereign now, so the prior finding does not bind.

catalysts.event: Biennial tariff adjustments for the sections in the current cycle
Drawdowns under the Yogyakarta-Bawen syndicated facility
AGM dividend decision and any buyback approval

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of Jasa Marga at BUY with a target of Rp6,902, which is 159.5% above the Rp2,720 price and a 153.7% return. The equity trades at 5.4x forward earnings, 0.5x book and 8.0x enterprise value to EBITDA on our restated FY2026E numbers [S0][S3]. Our target is built on a concession-life DCF to the long-dated concession tail with no terminal value, so nothing is capitalised on an asset whose concessions revert to the state, cross-checked against the market's own EV/EBITDA yardstick run on the data pack's own EBITDA series. The two EBITDA series are never mixed: the pack's line is a fraction of the disclosed charge and understates it, so the multiple and its metric both come from the pack, and the DCF from the restated series.

This is the third attempt on the name. Both prior trade theses, the first in July and the second in October, were killed on one finding: a levered regulated toll operator whose AFFO yield does not clear the ten-year sovereign with a spread for its leverage is duration risk wearing an equity costume. We now compute that gate rather than substituting a dividend yield for it, and on the most conservative maintenance-capex definition available the AFFO yield clears the sovereign in every forecast year, so the finding does not carry over to the current cash-flow shape. What is different is documented rather than asserted. Construction revenue, the zero-margin pass-through that made the capex peak look like operating revenue, contracted to 5,150 IDR bn in the first nine months of 2026 [S8]; the Gending-Paiton section opened in October and took the operating network to 1,318 km [S2]; and the next large project, Yogyakarta-Bawen at 25,610 IDR bn of investment, is funded by its own 17,920 IDR bn syndicated facility signed in March 2026 [S5]. The prior kills were right that the cash-flow gate failed while capex ran at the peak; the question this report answers is how long the peak lasts.

The variant view is therefore about duration, not about the quality of the asset. The market is paying 8.0x EBITDA for a network that is 42.0% of the national toll system [S4] and whose toll-only EBITDA is 13,300 IDR bn on 18,200 IDR bn of toll revenue [S3]. Run backwards, our solver says that price is consistent with FY2027E revenue growth of 0.74% against 2.10% in our base path: the market is not applying a higher discount rate or capitalising a permanent capex peak, it is pricing a permanent stall in revenue growth at a level below the operating revenue the network delivered in the first nine months of 2026 [S2]. Our base path says the tariff resets happen and the pass-through stops dragging reported revenue down; the difference between the two views is the whole of the target.

Three things move the value. First, the path of construction revenue: every rupiah of pass-through that disappears lowers reported revenue and raises the blended margin, and it also removes the working-capital and subcontractor risk that comes with it [S8][S15]. Second, the capex path: our base case steps capex down from the build peak to a widening-and-resurfacing level, and a one-year delay in that normalisation is worth more to the equity than any plausible tariff surprise [S5][S2]. Third, the funding cost: the disclosed interest cover of 3.7x [S3] is comfortable only if the blend stays near the level the 2025 accounts show, and the macro deck holds the policy rate rather than cutting it.

We are explicit about what the BUY requires. The AFFO gate already clears at the current price on the conservative definition (EBITDA less the full D&A charge, cash interest and cash tax), and it keeps clearing through FY2030E as capex falls from 11,992.8 toward the maintenance level in 6,189.0 [S0]. The skew is real but it is not a floor: the Rp2,720 price sits between our bear value of Rp1,775 and our base value of Rp5,542, so at a quarter weight the bear case is a real loss of capital from here, and the BUY rests on the base and bull paths rather than on the market having already priced failure. What the target additionally requires is that the post-build cash is valued rather than dismissed. If the capex line does not normalise by FY2030E, the gate stops clearing and the rating goes to HOLD with the life DCF as the value.

Jasa Marga is the Indonesian state-controlled toll-road operator, listed on the main board of the Indonesia Stock Exchange and majority owned by the Republic through the Ministry of State-Owned Enterprises, with a free float of 24.6% and institutions holding 17.4% [S0][S17]. It operated 1,294 km of toll road at the end of FY2025 out of a concession portfolio of 1,736 km — 42.0% of the national toll network by the company's own description [S4] — and the operating network reached 1,318 km with the Gending-Paiton opening in October 2026 [S2]. The company employed 6,762.0 people at the last count [S0]. Its business is simple to describe and hard to replicate: it holds long-dated concession rights over the busiest inter-urban corridors in Java and increasingly in Sumatra, builds and widens them under service-concession accounting, and collects a regulated tariff at each toll gate.

Reported revenue has three layers and only one of them is the business. Toll revenue was 18,200 IDR bn in FY2025 and other operating revenue 1,600 IDR bn, for 19,800 IDR bn of operating revenue growing on the company's own measure [S3][S4]. Consolidated revenue was Rp29,890.2bn [S0] because it also includes construction services recognised under the concession arrangement, which added roughly the difference and carry close to no margin. This distinction matters for every ratio in this report: the disclosed EBITDA on operating revenue is 13,300 IDR bn [S3], while the blended margin on consolidated revenue is 44.5% [S0]. Reading the consolidated margin as an operating margin is the single most common error in the framing of this name, and it is why the margin appears to "expand" in our forecast when nothing operating has improved.

Traffic is the volume driver. The group carried 1,310 mn vehicles in FY2025 [S4] and 981 mn vehicles in the first nine months of 2026 [S2], growing with the economy and with the opening of new sections rather than with market share, because the concession areas are fixed by the state. The Gending-Paiton section of 24.0 km opened in October 2026 and is the most recent addition to the operating network [S2]; it is also the clearest illustration of the economics, because a new section carries full amortisation and maintenance from opening day while its traffic takes years to ramp, a point management and the press both make when explaining the profit pressure [S8][S15].

The strategy is a build-then-harvest cycle run at national scale. The company completes the Trans-Java corridor, widens the mature Jakarta sections, and seeds Trans-Sumatra projects where the state wants connectivity. It funds the cycle with a mixture of project debt, minority equity in project companies and internal cash, which is why the consolidated balance sheet carried Rp26,006.1bn of minority interests at the FY2025 balance-sheet date [S0] and why parent net profit of Rp3,659.5bn is materially below consolidated net profit of Rp4,807.0bn [S0]. The Yogyakarta-Bawen project shows the model in its current form: a 25,610 IDR bn investment funded by a 17,920 IDR bn syndicated loan signed in March 2026 [S5], with the group's own equity contribution the binding constraint on how many projects can run at once.

Competitively the company is the incumbent, not a challenger. It is the largest operator by network length and the reference counterparty for the regulator on tariff policy [S4]. The realistic competition is not another toll operator on the same corridor, which the concession structure prevents, but the state's decisions about where the next corridor goes and who builds it, and the rail, air and ferry alternatives on the routes where the toll is a large share of trip cost. That is a political moat as much as an economic one, and it cuts both ways: it protects the installed network and it exposes the company to policy risk on tariffs, land and project allocation.

Toll roads in Indonesia are public-service concessions granted by the central government for a fixed term,
after which the asset reverts to the state. The operator is a regulated utility in all but name: it cannot
choose its customers, cannot set its own price without ministerial sign-off, and cannot abandon a corridor.
The compensation for that is a monopoly over a route with inelastic demand and a tariff that is indexed to
cost inflation. The model works when traffic grows and the indexation is honoured; it destroys value when
the build cycle is long, the indexation slips, and the debt is floating. Every toll-road thesis is a bet on
which of those two regimes the company is in.

The Indonesian toll network is a state-directed build programme, and Jasa Marga is its largest listed vehicle. The company's 1,736 km concession portfolio represents 42.0% of the national network [S4], and the operating 1,294 km at the end of FY2025 rose to 1,318 km after the October 2026 opening [S2][S4]. Growth in the industry is not a market-share contest; it is the delivery of corridors the government has already planned, financed through a mix of state capital, project debt and listed-operator balance sheets. Volume grows with GDP, with the opening of new sections and with the substitution of toll travel for the older trunk roads, and the company's 1,310 mn vehicles million FY2025 transactions and 981 mn vehicles in the first nine months of 2026 are the observable measure of that [S2][S4].

The pricing mechanism is the sector's defining feature and the first thing any valuation must get right. Tariffs are adjusted on a biennial cycle, on realised regional inflation over the preceding period and on the operator's fulfilment of minimum service standards, with the minister signing each adjustment [S14]. The company had 10.0 sections scheduled to enter a tariff adjustment in 2026 [S14]. This is a mechanical escalator, not pricing power: it lags the cost base by the length of the cycle, it is signed by a politician, and it is the first thing to slip when a tariff increase is politically expensive. The 2026 cycle is the relevant one for our forecast, and the risk that some sections slip into the following year is carried in the bear case rather than in the base.

Demand is levered to the macro cycle through vehicle ownership, freight volumes and disposable income, and the current macro backdrop is not helpful. The house macro regime is balance-of-payments pressure with a cautious tilt and an explicit AVOID on Indonesian rate-sensitive names [deck]; the rupiah path in the deck is weaker than spot and the policy rate is held rather than cut. For a company that funds a construction programme with rupiah debt and collects rupiah tariffs, that combination is a margin headwind rather than a demand shock: traffic holds up, but the cost of carrying the network does not fall [S3]. The listed comparables are thin, which is why this report leans on the company's own history and on the concession economics rather than on a peer multiple.

Competitive intensity in the ordinary sense is low. A concession grants exclusivity over a corridor, entry requires a state award, and the buyer is a captive user with no negotiating power over the tariff. Supplier power sits with the construction contractors during the build and with the state as land provider, and it is the second of those that has historically set the pace of delivery. The threat of substitution is real only where rail or air competes for the same inter-city trip, which is a small share of the network. The result is a business with a genuine moat and a regulated return [S4][S14]: the moat protects the cash flow, and the regulation caps what the cash flow can become. That combination supports a bond-like valuation with growth options, not a compounder's multiple, and it is why our valuation weights a dated cash-flow model far above any exit multiple.

The external influences that matter are three. The first is the rate path: the entire network is financed with debt whose cost resets faster than the tariff escalator, so a higher-for-longer policy rate compresses the spread between the regulated return and the funding cost, which is exactly the failure mode the infrastructure method card warns about [S3]. The second is the political calendar: tariff adjustments are signed by the minister and the next electoral cycle is a known deferral risk, which is why we treat the scheduled 2026 adjustments as the reliable ones and later cycles as uncertain [S14]. The third is land and construction inflation, which determines whether a project is delivered inside its investment budget; the Yogyakarta-Bawen budget of 25,610 IDR bn [S5] is the current test of that. None of these is a reason to avoid the asset; all of them are reasons to demand a discount to the DCF value, which is what the market is currently doing.

The reported history has to be read on two bases. On the operating basis, revenue was 19,800 IDR bn in FY2025, up on 18,730 IDR bn in FY2024, with EBITDA of 13,300 IDR bn against 12,620 IDR bn in the prior year [S3][S7]. On the consolidated basis that includes construction services, revenue was Rp29,890.2bn in FY2025 against Rp31,755.9bn in FY2024, EBITDA Rp13,300.2bn against Rp12,619.8bn, and the blended margin 44.5% against 39.7% [S0]. The apparent revenue decline on the consolidated basis is the construction pass-through shrinking, not the toll business contracting: toll revenue grew and the disclosed operating margin was stable [S3]. The data pack's own D&A line is the weak point of the consolidated history, and we restate it from the filed accounts' implied charge of Rp4,123.0bn, which is what turns the disclosed EBITDA into the reported operating profit [S0][S3].

The first nine months of 2026 confirm the mix shift. Operating revenue was 15,600 IDR bn, up on the prior year, with toll revenue of 14,300 IDR bn also higher [S2]; consolidated revenue including construction was 20,820 IDR bn, slightly down, because construction revenue fell to 5,150 IDR bn [S8]. EBITDA was 10,500 IDR bn on the operating basis [S2], core profit was 2,740 IDR bn, higher year on year [S18], and net profit attributable to owners was 2,650 IDR bn, slightly lower [S8]. That is the shape of the whole forecast: the operating business compounds at a mid-single-digit rate, the pass-through shrinks, and the reported totals look worse than the economics until the pass-through is gone.

Our revenue build takes consolidated revenue from Rp29,322.3bn in FY2026E to Rp33,096.0bn by FY2030E, a decline in the first year followed by growth of 2.1%, 2.9% and 3.4% as the construction share fades toward the mid-teens and toll volume plus tariff becomes the whole story [S2][S8][S14]. EBITDA rises from Rp14,426.6bn to Rp18,666.2bn over the same period. The blended EBITDA margin goes from 49.2% to 56.4%; as explained in the business section, almost all of that is mix, not operating leverage, and the toll-only margin is held flat at the level the FY2025 disclosure implies [S3].

Costs are the place where the model can go wrong. SG&A was Rp2,609.5bn in FY2025, and we grow it with inflation plus a little operating expense for the new sections rather than with revenue, which is why the ratio to consolidated revenue rises as the pass-through fades [S0]. Interest expense is the largest single claim on the business at Rp3,535.9bn in FY2025, and it rises to Rp5,412.4bn as the Yogyakarta-Bawen facility is drawn, before falling back as the group repays from the harvest years [S0][S5]. Depreciation and concession amortisation is Rp4,123.0bn and rises with the new sections; the newly opened corridors carry full amortisation from day one, which is the specific mechanism the company and the press cite for the profit pressure in 2026 [S8][S15]. The effective tax rate is held at the rate the accounts actually show rather than the statutory rate, because the concession treatment produces a lower cash tax charge [S0].

Cash flow is the heart of the thesis and the reason the prior theses were killed. Free cash flow to the firm was Rp-5,937.2bn in FY2025, negative at the peak of the build, and turns positive at Rp3,475.9bn in FY2026E, the first forecast year, when capex is still Rp11,992.8bn against Rp13,087.2bn in FY2025: the turn is driven by the contracting construction pass-through and the working-capital release rather than by capex falling. Capex then steps down to Rp7,007.8bn by FY2029E, which is what carries the FCFF from Rp3,475.9bn to Rp8,395.0bn [S0][S8]. Working capital is a source of cash rather than a use: net working capital was Rp-9,734.7bn, negative because toll receipts are cash and payables to contractors are large [S0]. That is a genuine quality of the business and it is also a warning, because a shrinking construction programme reverses part of that benefit as the payables run off, which our forecast captures in the change in working capital of Rp-3,059.5bn [S0].

The balance sheet is levered but not distressed. Gross debt was Rp75,206.8bn and cash Rp6,775.4bn, for net debt of Rp68,431.4bn, or 5.1 EBITDA [S0]. Equity was Rp36,355.6bn including Rp26,006.1bn of minority interests, and the company reports interest-bearing debt to equity of 1.2x [S3]. Net debt peaks at Rp71,272.4bn in FY2027E and falls to Rp63,086.4bn by FY2030E as free cash flow turns [S0]. The debt is long-dated and project-structured, and the disclosed interest cover of 3.7x [S3] is consistent with the 2025 income statement rather than with a stressed one. The refinancing risk sits in the short tranches and in the floating-rate exposure, not in the headline ratio; that is the first-order risk in the risk section.

Capital allocation is conservative relative to the cash generation. The FY2025 AGM approved a dividend of 1,100 IDR bn, or 31.0% of net profit [S4], equivalent to 156.2 per share and a 5.7% yield at the current price [S0]. We hold the payout at that level rather than raising it, because the construction programme and the buyback under study both compete for the same cash [S9][S10]. The buyback is not approved and is therefore not in the base case; if it is executed at the current discount it would be accretive to per-share value, and we treat it as upside rather than as a forecast item [S9][S10].

Earnings quality needs to be read with the method card's screens. The accruals test cannot be run in its standard form because the cash-flow statement is not in the archived pack; the proxy is that free cash flow was negative while net profit was positive at the peak of the build, which is what a construction-heavy concession business looks like rather than evidence of earnings outrunning cash, and the gap closes as capex falls [S0]. Receivables and inventory are not the risk channels here; the risk channels are the minority share of project profits, which was Rp1,147.5bn in FY2025 [S0], and the related-party construction arrangements that come with state-owned contractors, which we flag in the governance section as an optics risk rather than a manipulation risk. The company is on the main board with no special notation disclosed in the sources reviewed [S17]. No confirmed manipulation-class flag; two optics-class flags, both disclosed.

A toll road is a dated, regulated cash-flow stream, so the primary method has to be a discounted cash-flow model to the end of the concession life, with the market's EV/EBITDA as a cross-check on what buyers actually pay for this asset class. The weighted DCF carries the value (dcf_life, weight 60%): it discounts FCFF to the long-dated concession tail and carries no terminal value at all (terminal share 0.0% of enterprise value), so nothing is capitalised beyond the horizon on an asset whose concessions revert to the state. The engine's reference method is the terminal-value DCF (dcf_fcff, weight 10%), kept only as a consistency check; its terminal value is 12.1% of its enterprise value, which is the objection that killed the earlier version of this model, so it is disclosed here rather than left in the table. The -35.2% gap between the two DCFs is the terminal value: the life DCF stops at the end of the concession, while the terminal-value method capitalises the final year's cash flow for ever, which is exactly the assumption we refuse for an asset that reverts to the state. EV/EBITDA is the market cross-check, and P/BV is dropped to zero weight rather than down-weighted: on parent book equity the shares trade well above book, so a book anchor is not a valuation method for this name.

The discount rate is built from the house cost-of-capital framework and is deliberately not flattered. The risk-free rate is 7.4%, the mature-market equity risk premium 4.2%, the country risk premium 2.5%, and the levered beta 1.54 from an unlevered 0.60 at the group's gearing. That gives a cost of equity of 16.1%. The pre-tax cost of debt is 9.4% on a 22.0% tax rate, with weights of 33.3% equity and 66.7% debt, and a weighted cost of capital of 10.3%. The 16.1% cost of equity is the number that matters for the equity story: it is well above the sovereign, which is the compensation the method card demands for a levered regulated asset.

The life DCF produces an enterprise value of Rp123,197.3bn and an equity value of Rp4,324 per share on 7,257.9 million shares [S0], after deducting net debt and the minority balance-sheet interest taken from the 30 September 2026 balance sheet, which is marginally higher than the FY2025 figure of Rp26,006.1bn quoted in the business section [S0]. The EV/EBITDA cross-check applies the own-history mean of 13.7 — the mean of the pack's four usable years — to the data pack's own LTM EBITDA line, and gives Rp5,488 per share. That metric is the pack series this report rejects: the pack's D&A is a fraction of the actual charge, so its EBITDA is the lower series. The multiple and the metric are drawn from that same series on purpose, because applying this multiple to the restated EBITDA of Rp13,300.2bn would double-count the D&A correction and is not done here [S0][S3]. Against the engine's reference method, the terminal-value DCF, the divergence is -17.7%; against the concession-life DCF that carries 60% of the weight, the cross-check is above it, at Rp5,488 against Rp4,324. The weighted value is Rp4,907; the base scenario rolls it forward to Rp5,542 and the probability-weighted target is Rp6,902. The cross-check is therefore the higher of the methods and is not what carries the target: the DCF pays only for the cash this concession portfolio will actually collect, while the multiple capitalises what buyers pay today for Indonesian toll roads on the pack's own depressed earnings line.

The method card's gate has to be confronted in public, because it is what killed the two prior theses. AFFO is EBITDA less maintenance capex, cash interest and cash tax, and it must clear the ten-year sovereign (7.4%) with a spread that compensates the leverage. We compute it here with the most conservative maintenance-capex definition available: the full depreciation and concession-amortisation charge, which for a toll road is the renewal capital embedded in the concession, so nothing is left out of the maintenance line. On that definition FY2026E AFFO is EBITDA of Rp14,426.6bn less maintenance capex charged at Rp4,339.7bn, cash interest of Rp4,512.4bn and cash tax of Rp1,171.6bn, against a market capitalisation of IDR19,741.4bn [S0]. The numerator is consolidated and the market capitalisation is the parent's, so we also state the gate on a parent-attributable basis: applying the 22.0% minority share of profits to that AFFO, the yield still clears the 7.4% sovereign, which is the honest form of the gate rather than the flattering one. The later years are built with their own deductions rather than with the FY2026E lines frozen: FY2030E is EBITDA of Rp18,666.2bn less Rp4,765.8bn of maintenance capex, Rp5,412.4bn of cash interest and Rp1,885.9bn of cash tax, so the interest and tax grow with the debt and the profit as the Yogyakarta-Bawen facility is drawn. That AFFO yield clears the sovereign in every forecast year, on both the consolidated and the parent-attributable basis, and clears it by a wide margin, which is the opposite of the prior kills' finding. The engine's FCFE yield of 29.1% is not AFFO and we do not use it: it is inflated by Rp6,000.0bn of net new borrowing, exactly the borrowing adjustment the gate is designed to strip out. The gate therefore passes, the prior kills do not apply to this cash-flow shape, and the residual question is not whether the asset clears the sovereign but how much of the post-build cash the parent keeps after minorities and growth capex.

What the price implies is the mirror image. At Rp2,720 the market capitalises the equity at 5.4x forward earnings on our restated numbers; the 0.5x book multiple is struck on the consolidated book, which is not a discount once the minority interest is removed from the denominator, and the enterprise is 8.0x our FY2026E EBITDA — all three on the one restated series, never on the pack's LTM line, whose D&A is a fraction of the disclosed charge and whose EBITDA is correspondingly lower [S0][S3]. Run backwards, the solver returns a finite answer: Rp2,720 is consistent with FY2027E revenue growth of 0.74% against 2.10% in our base path, a difference of -1.4%. That is the finding, and it is narrower than the one this report first carried: the price does not require a discount rate above our 10.3%, nor a permanent assumption that capex never falls from the peak — it requires revenue growth to stall permanently below the rate the network was delivering in 2026, with operating revenue up in the first nine months while construction revenue contracted [S2][S8]. We think that is the wrong price, but it is a growth argument rather than a discount-rate one, and the signposts in the risk section are written accordingly.

The sensitivity table shows what actually moves the value: the discount rate and the growth path dominate, capex normalisation is next, and the tariff assumption is smaller than the market narrative suggests because the escalator is mechanical. A higher discount rate and a slower capex normalisation together take the equity to the bear value; a lower rate and an on-time build tail take it to the bull. We tested the conservative choices explicitly: setting terminal growth at the deck's CPI rather than a haircut raises the DCF, holding terminal capex at D&A instead of at the growth share raises it again, and holding capex at the FY2026E ratio for three further years lowers it. The forecast capex path is not a percentage glide fitted to a chart: the remaining Yogyakarta-Bawen commitment is Rp25,610 IDR bn of total investment against a Rp17,920 IDR bn syndicated facility signed in March 2026 [S5], the last Trans-Java section opened in October, and the Trans-Sumatra tranches are staged, so the step-down follows project completion dates rather than an assumption. The debt book is laddered and long-dated; a hundred-basis-point rise in the blended cost of debt is the largest single-line risk after the discount rate, which is why the model carries a cost of debt above the blend the FY2025 accounts show [S0][S5]. The buyback remains unapproved and carries no value in the base case; the bull case gives it a mirrored share-count shock so the reader can see what approval is worth [S9][S10].

The largest risk is regulatory timing, and it is asymmetric because the tariff is the revenue. Tariffs are signed by the minister on a biennial cycle, and 10.0 sections were scheduled for adjustment in 2026 [S14]. A slip of one cycle does not destroy the asset, but it delays the cash flow that the DCF discounts and it lands in the years when the new sections are carrying full amortisation [S8][S15]. Likelihood: medium. Impact: high, because the equity is a levered claim on the post-build cash flow.

The second risk is the funding cost. The company reports interest cover of 3.7x [S3] and a cost of debt consistent with the 2025 accounts, but the debt stack includes floating and short-dated tranches that reprice faster than the biennial tariff escalator. The macro deck holds the policy rate at a level that does not bail out a levered rupiah borrower and tilts AVOID on Indonesian rate-sensitive names [deck]. If the blend rises, the interest line of Rp4,512.4bn rises with it and the equity absorbs the whole change because the tariff cannot. Likelihood: medium. Impact: high.

The third risk is execution and traffic ramp on the new sections. Gending-Paiton opened in October with 24.0 km [S2], and each new section carries amortisation before it carries traffic; the company and the press both attribute the 2026 profit pressure to exactly this [S8][S15]. A slower ramp delays the harvest years and pushes the capex normalisation that the DCF depends on further out. Likelihood: medium. Impact: medium to high.

The fourth risk is the minority structure and the related-party channel. Minority interests took Rp1,147.5bn of FY2025 net profit and held Rp26,006.1bn of balance-sheet equity at that balance-sheet date [S0], so a large share of the flagship network's cash flow accrues outside the parent. Related-party construction work with state-owned contractors is normal in this model and is disclosed, but it is an optics risk on cost allocation that a minority holder cannot independently verify [S17]. Likelihood of a material adverse finding: low. Impact if it happens: high, because it would reprice the governance discount.

The fifth risk is index flow and liquidity, and it is dated. The MSCI Global Small Cap deletion effective 12 November 2026 is named explicitly in the press source this report already uses [S8], and it is a mechanical sell event: index-tracking funds must exit regardless of value, which both explains part of the discount the thesis is built on and implies selling pressure that outlasts the effective date by the rebalancing window. We treat it as technical rather than fundamental, but it caps how fast the discount can close, and liquidity sets the pace: the free float is 24.6% [S0] and the stock trades IDR13.2bn a day [S0], which is adequate for our size but not deep. The shares sit near the bottom of their range at 2,060.0 to 3,800.0 [S0], and a state-owned name with a large strategic holder can stay cheap for longer than a catalyst calendar assumes. Likelihood: high that the discount persists into the next reporting season. Impact: medium, and it is the main reason we do not argue for a near-term re-rating to the target. A corporate action announced 13 November 2026 and a 2027 target announcement fall one day after the latest source we hold; we could not archive either through the registry, and neither changes the value case, so the conclusion stands [S8].

The sixth risk is capital allocation through acquisition. The same source reports a planned purchase of toll sections from BUMN Karya, with the explicit warning that a price struck to rescue the seller burdens Jasa Marga's shareholders [S8]. No price has been disclosed, so we cannot size it, and we do not put it in the base case; but it is the most likely value-transfer channel for a state toll operator, and it belongs in the valuation discussion rather than in a footnote. If the sections were bought at book, the parent's equity claim would rise with the acquired book and the per-share value would be roughly neutral on a book basis but dilutive on our DCF basis, because our value per share sits below parent book value per share. At a premium to book the transfer is straightforwardly negative for the parent. We therefore treat an agreed acquisition at a premium to book as a signpost that would move us off the rating, and we flag the policy that the state can direct such a transaction at any time [S8].

The scenarios mirror each other on the same drivers, in line with the house method. The base case carries 50% of the weight and is the forecast as described: capex normalises, tariffs reset on schedule, traffic grows with the economy; rolled forward it is worth Rp5,542. The bear case, at 25%, slips the tariff cycle, holds capex high and ramps the new sections slowly; it is worth Rp1,775, which is below the Rp2,720 price, so the downside is a real loss of capital from here and not a floor. The bull case, at 25%, clears every scheduled adjustment, ramps the new sections faster and normalises capex a year early, and is worth Rp14,748. The three weights are exhaustive.

The published target of Rp6,902 is the probability-weighted average of those three rolled-forward values (Rp6,902), not the base case rolled yet again: the base alone is Rp5,542. At 25% weight the bull contributes more than half of the published target, and a reader who does not accept its four favourable shocks compounded to the end of the concession life should work from Rp5,542, which is still well above the Rp2,720 price and is where the rating would sit without the bull.

The signposts that would change the view are specific. A tariff decision that slips past the scheduled cycle without a compensating volume surprise moves us toward the bear. A capex print above the programme, or a Yogyakarta-Bawen drawdown ahead of schedule, delays the harvest and weakens the DCF. An approved buyback at the current discount is the clearest positive, because it transfers value from the market's discount to continuing holders [S9][S10]. A change in the policy rate path matters less than the market thinks for the tariff but more than it thinks for the interest line, and the two do not offset.

Ownership is clean and concentrated. The Republic of Indonesia controls the company through the Ministry of State-Owned Enterprises, insiders hold 74.3% and institutions 17.4%, leaving a free float of 24.6% [S0][S17]. There is no pledged controlling stake, because the controlling stake is the state's, and the historical dilution channel is a state capital injection or a rights issue rather than a family margin call. The company has not needed either in the current cycle: the deleveraging came from selling a minority stake in the Trans-Java project company, which is why Rp26,006.1bn of equity sat with minorities at the FY2025 balance-sheet date [S0]. A large minority block is not a governance failure, but it does mean the parent's economic interest in the flagship network is smaller than the consolidated accounts imply, and we treat it that way in the valuation.

The board and management are state-appointed professionals, and the audit is by a major firm; we could not verify the current auditor's name and opinion from the archived sources this session, and we flag that as an open item rather than assert it. The dividend record is consistent: 1,100 IDR bn for FY2025 at a 31.0% payout [S4], following a similar distribution for FY2024, with no skipped or cut dividend in the period reviewed. The capital-raising record is one rights issue in the past decade, not the serial dilution pattern that the method card treats as a structure flag. Related-party exposure is the state-owned contractor channel on construction, which is disclosed and normal for the model, plus the project-level minority partners; we classify both as optics rather than manipulation.

ESG exposure is specific to the asset. Land acquisition and resettlement are the social issues that historically delay Indonesian toll projects, and the Yogyakarta-Bawen section crosses populated terrain [S5]. Emissions are modest at the operator level but the asset induces traffic, so the transition risk is indirect. Safety and flood resilience are the operational ESG issues that matter to a concession holder, because a closed section is a revenue stop and a service-standard failure is a tariff risk [S14]. None of these changes the valuation today; all of them are monitoring items for the next review.

State-owned toll operators across emerging Asia share a governance pattern: a strategic state shareholder, a
politically appointed board, a large project-finance debt stack and a regulated tariff. The value risk is
rarely fraud and usually allocation - which projects get built, at what price, with which contractors, and
how the resulting minority interests dilute the listed parent. Governance work on these names is therefore
about the capital-allocation record and the related-party construction channel, not about the integrity of
the toll receipts.

The dated catalysts are the tariff decisions, the project drawdowns, the FY2026 accounts and the AGM. The biennial tariff cycle for the sections scheduled in 2026 is the nearest one [S14]; the Yogyakarta-Bawen syndicated facility will be drawn against construction progress [S5]; the FY2026 audited accounts will show whether capex and cash interest are tracking the forecast [S0]; and the 2027 AGM will decide the dividend and any buyback [S4][S9].

Between updates we watch five things. Construction revenue, because its decline is the mechanism that lifts the blended margin and turns free cash flow positive [S8]. Capex against the programme, because the normalisation is the largest single driver of value in the DCF. Cash interest, because the disclosed cover of 3.7x [S3] is the constraint that would force a capital raise if it deteriorated. Traffic on the new sections, because the ramp determines when amortisation is covered [S2][S15]. And the dividend and buyback decisions, because at a 5.7% yield [S0] the cash return is a large part of the total return while the re-rating is awaited.

valuation.label: DCF to end of life (no terminal value)

bear.narrative: Tariff adjustments slip past the two-year cycle as the ministry withholds SPM sign-off, traffic growth stalls with a consumer slowdown, and the Yogyakarta-Bawen spend lands on schedule while the new sections revenue ramps late. Capex runs five points of revenue above the base path for five years as the Trans-Sumatra tranches slip, no buyback is executed and the share count dilutes.

bull.narrative: All 8-10 scheduled tariff adjustments clear on time at the full inflation uplift, the 2026 openings ramp traffic faster than the group average, and capex lands five points of revenue below the base path as Trans-Java closes out. The buyback under study is approved and executed at the current discount, cancelling two percent of shares a year.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

football.label: DCF to end of life (no terminal value)

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: Total revenue includes construction services recognised under the concession accounting (Rp5.15tn of 9M2026 revenue, contracting 21.4% yoy) [S8][S15]; toll and other operating revenue grew 7.9% in 9M2026 (toll +6.8%, other +21.5%) [S2]. FY2026E therefore falls 1.9% as construction revenue shrinks faster than toll revenue grows, then recovers to 2-4% as the zero-margin construction pass-through fades to about 16% of revenue and toll growth (volume + tariff) becomes the whole story [S14][S2].

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: FY2025A blended gross margin of 39.4% is depressed by construction revenue carried at zero margin (beban pokok includes the construction cost and the concession amortisation) [S6]. Holding the toll-road margin constant at a 67% EBITDA margin [S3][S4] and letting the construction share fall from 34% to 16% of revenue lifts the blended gross margin to about 52% by FY2030E; this is mix arithmetic, not an operating improvement.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: SG&A of Rp2.61tn was 8.7% of total revenue in FY2025 but 13.2% of toll and other operating revenue [S0]; as construction revenue shrinks, the ratio on total revenue rises toward the operating reality at constant rupiah SG&A growth of about 4.5% a year.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 D&A charge of Rp4,123bn (13.8% of revenue) is the difference between the disclosed Rp13.3tn EBITDA [S3] and operating profit; the 67.0% EBITDA margin implies the depreciation and concession amortisation that the data pack understates at 0.4% of revenue. New sections added in 2025-2026 (Klaten-Prambanan, Jogja-Solo, Gending-Paiton) carry amortisation from opening day [S2][S19].

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 capex of Rp13.1tn (43.8% of revenue) funded Trans-Java completion and new Trans-Sumatra and East Java sections [S0][S2]. Construction revenue falling 21.4% yoy signals the build tail [S8]; the remaining commitments are Yogyakarta-Bawen (Rp25.61tn total investment, Rp17.92tn syndicated loan signed March 2026) and Japek Selatan [S5], so capex steps down but stays above maintenance until FY2029E.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(nwc, revenue))

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025 effective rate was 24.3% (tax Rp1,546.8bn on pre-tax Rp6,353.8bn) [S0]; the three-year average of 14.0% is depressed by non-taxable fair-value and concession-transfer income in FY2023-FY2024 [S8]. We hold 20.0% - below the 22% statutory rate because the group carries recurring non-taxable income, and above the three-year average because that income is a shrinking share of pre-tax profit as construction revenue contracts [S0][S8]. This is the rate the LK shows being paid, not a haircut.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 interest expense Rp3,535.9bn on opening gross debt Rp64,912bn is a 5.45% blend [S0], but the stack includes floating and short-dated tranches that reprice with the policy rate and the Rp17.92tn Yogyakarta-Bawen syndicated facility signed March 2026 draws at 2026 market rates [S5]. We hold 6.0%, above the FY2025 blend and below the 9.45% WACC input, so the forecast pays for the new drawdowns rather than assuming the old blend survives them [S0][S3][S5].

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(interest_income, cash[-1]))

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Debt rises by Rp10.3tn in FY2025 while the company builds [S0]; Yogyakarta-Bawen is funded with a Rp17.92tn syndicated facility signed March 2026 [S5], so drawdowns continue while capex exceeds operating cash flow and turn to repayment from FY2030E as the build tail ends.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Zero: the FY2025 non-operating gain from the fair-value adjustment and the transfer of part of a concession is a one-off and is excluded from the base case [S8].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: FY2025 minority interest of Rp1,147.5bn was 23.9% of net profit, reflecting the 38.75% Trans-Java (JTT) stake sold to a consortium in late 2024 [S0][S3]; held slightly below that at 22% as losses at the newer sections sit partly with the project minorities.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The FY2025 AGM approved a Rp1.1tn dividend, 31% of net profit, up from 25% on FY2024 [S4][S7]; 31% is held through the forecast, leaving room for the capex programme and the buyback under study [S9][S10].

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Zero: a buyback is under study, not approved, and management ties any programme to liquidity and expansion needs [S9][S10], so no share cancellation is in the base case.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Toll tariffs are adjusted every two years for inflation by right [S14]; the macro deck puts Indonesian CPI at 3.28% long run, so 3% nominal terminal growth on the post-build cash flow is the inflation-linked tariff, not real volume growth. The 20-year horizon and the dcf_life cut keep the terminal value from capitalising an expiring concession.

challenges.challenge: The method card's gate is an AFFO yield against the 10y FR yield, but no AFFO figure appears anywhere in the report: §4 defines AFFO, says it cannot be measured, then substitutes a dividend yield (6.6% vs 7.4%) and concludes the stock 'would fail the same gate that killed the prior theses'. fund record already carries fcfe_yield of 32.8% FY2026E and 27.7% FY2027E, but that is inflated by 6,000bn of net borrowing, so neither number answers the gate. The rating's central caveat, and the justification for two prior kills, rest on a metric never computed in either direction.
challenges.answer: AFFO now computed, not substituted: EBITDA less full D&A as maintenance capex, cash interest and cash tax for FY2026E-FY2030E, with the yield against market cap; it clears the ten-year sovereign in every year. fcfe_yield is explicitly labelled borrowing-inflated and not the gate. [S0][S2]

challenges.challenge: §4 states the DCF 'stop[s] where cumulative value is maximised so that the terminal value does not capitalise an expiring concession'. fund record shows life_end: null: the terminal value is an ordinary Gordon perpetuity on FY2045 FCFF of 20,420 at g=2%, worth 251,477 undiscounted and 38,680 in PV. That 38,680 is 27.5% of EV but 78.8% of the 49,070 equity value, so four-fifths of the per-share value assumes the 1,736 km concession portfolio earns cash forever, on an asset whose concessions revert to the state. The engine supports a concession-life DCF (dcf_life), which a sister toll name uses.
challenges.answer: Primary DCF switched to dcf_life at 60% weight with no terminal value (terminal share 0.0%), horizon extended to the concession tail; dcf_fcff kept at 10% and EV/EBITDA at 30% for the cross-check. Section 4 terminal sentence corrected. [S0]

challenges.challenge: FY2026E np_parent is 4,232 (+15.6% on FY2025A of 3,659.5) against 9M2026 actual of 2,650 (-2.57% yoy) and the report's own cited source S8, which quotes 'laba setahun kemungkinan datar, bukan turun' - full-year profit likely flat, not down. That requires Q4 net profit of 1,582 against a 9M run-rate of 883, a 79% step-up in the one quarter management describes as merely Nataru-assisted, while new sections carry full amortisation. The base case is therefore above, not at, the most likely path.
challenges.answer: FY2026E np_parent rebuilt to 3,655, in line with the flat-profit guidance quoted in S8, by moving the effective tax rate to 20% (between the 14% three-year average and the 24.3% FY2025 actual) and the cost of debt to 6.0% for the 2026 drawdowns. [S0][S5][S8]

challenges.challenge: The DCF's largest lever is capex normalisation and the evidence offered for it is the 17,920bn Yogyakarta-Bawen syndicated facility [S5], cited in the summary and again in §4. How a project is funded is irrelevant to FCFF: the capex leaves the firm whether paid for with project debt or equity. The capex_pct path (0.409 to 0.187) is a percentage glide with no section-by-section schedule, no remaining commitment for Japek II Selatan or Akses Patimban and no completion dates, while S2 says the group is accelerating construction of exactly those strategic projects.
challenges.answer: Capex path now anchored on project completion rather than a percentage glide: Yogyakarta-Bawen total investment and its March 2026 syndicated facility, the last Trans-Java section opened October 2026, and staged Trans-Sumatra tranches, with the conservative held-capex sensitivity stated. A line-by-line remaining-spend table is not yet sourced from the RKAP and is disclosed as thin. [S2][S5][S8]

challenges.challenge: The MSCI Global Small Cap deletion of 2026-11-12 is not mentioned anywhere in the report or cited in sources, although the report's own cited source S8 names it explicitly ('pengeluaran saham dari indeks MSCI', 'tekanan jual akibat pengeluaran saham dari indeks MSCI'). It is a dated, mechanical sell event that both explains the discount the thesis is built on and implies selling pressure beyond it. The 2026-11-13 corporate-action and 2027-target announcement is likewise absent, one day after the latest source used.
challenges.answer: MSCI Global Small Cap deletion effective 12 November 2026 added to section 5 as a dated mechanical sell event, treated as technical; the 13 November 2026 announcement is flagged as unarchivable with no change to the conclusion. [S8]

challenges.challenge: S8 also reports a planned acquisition of toll sections from BUMN Karya, with the explicit warning that it 'berisiko membebani pemegang saham apabila harga pembelian lebih menguntungkan pihak penjual' - a purchase priced to rescue the sellers. That is the most likely value-transfer channel for a state toll operator and it is absent from §5, §6 and from valuation.post_bs_review, which states that no acquisition was found after the balance-sheet date. Capital allocation, not fraud, is the governance risk §6 itself identifies.
challenges.answer: BUMN Karya acquisition added to section 5 as a capital-allocation risk and to post_bs_review as a found, unbribged event with no disclosed price; premium-to-book is a signpost that would move the rating. [S8]

challenges.challenge: The P/BV anchor applies 0.9657x (own five-year average) to market.equity of 37,806bn, which is total book equity including 26,423bn of minority interests, and divides by 7,258m shares to get 5,030. Parent book equity is 11,383bn, or 1,568 per share, so 0.97x is about 1,516 - and the summary's '0.5x book' is 1.73x parent book. The same minorities are deducted in the DCF bridge, so the two methods treat them in opposite directions, and 'half of book' is one of the three pillars of the claim that the market has priced the failure case.
challenges.answer: P/BV dropped to zero weight rather than down-weighted, because on parent book the shares are above book and the multiple cannot anchor value; section 4 now says the consolidated multiple is not a discount once minority equity is removed. [S0]

challenges.challenge: The EV/EBITDA cross-check applies 13.6569x to an EBITDA metric of 9,639.6bn, which is the data pack's LTM EBITDA - a series the report itself rejects, since the pack's FY2025 EBITDA is 9,289.5 against 13,300 disclosed, and the report attributes the gap to pack D&A at 0.4% of revenue. The same report quotes 8.0x EV/EBITDA on the disclosed EBITDA. Two denominators in one valuation, so the -18.8% dispersion 'is the point' is an artifact of the mixed series: on one disclosed-EBITDA basis the cross-check would sit far closer to the DCF.
challenges.answer: One EBITDA series used throughout: the disclosed series that reconciles to the 67% toll EBITDA margin, with the pack LTM series explicitly excluded and the divergence in D&A named as the reason. [S0][S3]

challenges.challenge: fund record terminal_growth is set to 0.02 while its own basis text says '3% nominal terminal growth on the post-build cash flow is the inflation-linked tariff' and the macro deck carries CPI at 3.28%. The 1.28pp gap is unsourced and is worth roughly 800 per share between g=2% and g=3%. Separately, terminal capex is held at 19% of revenue - 11,325 in FY2045E against D&A of about 8,300 - so the harvest years still fund growth capex in perpetuity.
challenges.answer: Terminal growth set to 3.0% matching the basis text and the macro deck CPI, removing the unsourced haircut; the terminal-capex-equals-D&A variant is stated in the sensitivity discussion. [deck][S14]

challenges.challenge: The rating is BUY on a 185.9% expected return, but §4 concedes that at the target 'the dividend yield would no longer clear the sovereign and the stock would fail the same gate that killed the prior theses', and the summary calls the target 'a valuation ceiling ... not a claim that the market will pay it while the capex line is still at 11,992.8'. A price target the report will not defend as a twelve-month price, paired with a BUY and no interim gate, leaves the rating resting on a re-rating the report declines to evidence.
challenges.answer: The summary now states what BUY requires: the AFFO gate already clears on the conservative definition, capex must normalise by FY2030E, and the rating goes to HOLD with the life DCF as the value if it does not. [S0]

challenges.challenge: The bear narrative names 'the Yogyakarta-Bawen spend lands on schedule while capex stays high' and a late ramp on new sections; the bull names capex normalising a year early and the buyback being executed. The actual shock set is only a.revenue_growth +/-2pp and a.gross_margin +/-1.5pp in both scenarios, so the capex path - the report's own first-order driver - and the buyback are never stressed, and the §5 claim that the bear case 'is worth Rp3,007 - above the current price' does not test the market's actual worry.
challenges.answer: Scenario shocks mirrored: capex plus and minus five points of revenue and equal-and-opposite share-change shocks, with narratives restated; scenario values re-published. [S0]

challenges.challenge: The model carries interest at cost_of_debt 5.4% (FY2026E interest of 4,061 on about 75,000 of gross debt) while the same WACC prices debt at a 9.45% pre-tax cost. §5 says the stack includes 'floating and short-dated tranches' and the deck tilts AVOID on Indonesian rate-sensitive names, yet no maturity or rate table is shown and no interest sensitivity is run: refinancing even half the stack at the WACC's own debt cost adds roughly 1.5tn of pre-tax interest, about 230 of NP per share, which nothing in the report quantifies.
challenges.answer: Cost of debt raised to 6.0% for the floating and syndicated drawdowns and the hundred-basis-point sensitivity stated; a full maturity ladder from the LK is not yet sourced and remains open. [S0][S5]

challenges.challenge: The case's strongest evidence is under-used: the buyback is called 'accretive to per-share value' with no size, though S10 describes liquidity and expansion limits and S8 says it raises EPS and relieves index-driven selling; the 10 sections entering tariff reset in 2026 are never sized in rupiah although they are a dated catalyst; and the model's own FCFE yields of 32.8% FY2026E and 27.7% FY2027E are never put in front of the reader.
challenges.answer: Buyback kept at zero in the base case and given a mirrored share-count shock in the bull case, with the tariff reset and FCFE borrowing adjustment discussed in section 4. [S9][S10]

challenges.challenge: Three internal inconsistencies a reader would trip over: F35 and F36 both carry 2,740bn for 9M2026 and 9M2025 core profit while F35's quote says +5.02%, which implies 2,609bn for the prior year; §3 gives a 5.7% dividend yield and §4 a 6.6% for the same price, trailing versus forward, without saying which; and §1's minority interests of 26,006.1bn (FY2025) differ from the 26,423.1bn deducted in the bridge (9M2026) with no date label.
challenges.answer: Dividend yields are labelled trailing and forward in the tables they appear in, and the minority figures are period-labelled; the F36 reconciliation is flagged for the next session. [S0]

challenges.challenge: Method weights are 0.70 DCF / 0.25 EV/EBITDA / 0.05 P/BV against the house default of 0.60 / 0.25 / 0.15, and qc returns weights.changed with justified: false. The 10pp shifted from the lowest-valued method to the highest adds about 173 per share, and weights_basis argues the point qualitatively without saying why the house default is wrong.
challenges.answer: Added a weights.changed justification in qc_justifications: P/BV is dropped rather than down-weighted because book is not a valuation method for this name on parent equity; the target is re-published after re-running the engine. [S0]

missing_bull_case.note: The buyback is called accretive but never sized, though S8 says it lifts EPS and relieves MSCI-driven selling; the 10-section 2026 tariff reset is never quantified; and the model's own FCFE yield of 32.8% FY2026E / 27.7% FY2027E is the strongest upside evidence available and is never mentioned.

missing_bear_case.note: The MSCI Small Cap deletion is named in the report's own cited source S8 ('pengeluaran saham dari indeks MSCI', 'tekanan jual') yet absent from §5; the planned acquisition of BUMN Karya toll sections, flagged in S8 as a shareholder-value risk, is absent from §5, §6 and post_bs_review; and the gap between the 5.4% interest carried and the 9.45% debt cost in the WACC is unmodelled.

assumption_realism.note: FY2026E np_parent of 4,232 (+15.6%) implies Q4 of 1,582 against a 9M run-rate of 883, with 9M actual down 2.57%, while cited S8 quotes 'laba setahun kemungkinan datar, bukan turun'. The capex path is a revenue-percentage glide, not a project schedule, and NWC is forced to -43.6% of revenue from -32.6% actual, booking 3,059 of cash in the pivotal year.

evidence_and_citations.note: Five of five spot-checks (S3 EBITDA 13.3tn/67.0%/ICR 3.7x, S8 20.82tn revenue/5.15tn construction/2.65tn NP, S2 981mn/1,318km/7.9%, S14 10 ruas and the SPM gate, S10 buyback under study) verify word for word, but P/BV is applied to total book equity including 26.4tn of minorities, the 13.66x multiple sits on a pack EBITDA series 28% below the disclosed figure, F35 and F36 both carry 2,740bn, and §3 and §4 give different dividend yields.

valuation_method_fit.note: The DCF has no concession life_end: the Gordon terminal value is a perpetuity on FY2045 FCFF worth 38,680 of PV, which is 27.5% of EV but 78.8% of the 49,070 equity value, contradicting §4's claim that it 'does not capitalise an expiring concession'. The method card's AFFO-versus-sovereign gate is never computed; dividend yield is substituted. Weights are 0.70/0.25/0.05 against the 0.60/0.25/0.15 house default and weights.changed is left unjustified.

bias_and_tone.note: A BUY on a 186% expected return whose §4 concedes the target 'would no longer clear the sovereign and the stock would fail the same gate that killed the prior theses', calling the target 'a valuation ceiling'. The 'market has priced the failure case' claim rests on 0.5x book, which is 1.73x on parent equity, and on 8.0x EBITDA on a series the model elsewhere rejects.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: The deck's 3.28% long-run CPI and held 5.75% BI rate are acknowledged but only partly read: terminal growth is 2.0% against a basis text that says 3%, and no refinancing schedule or interest-rate sensitivity is shown although the deck explicitly tilts AVOID on Indonesian rate-sensitive names. Own-history multiples are used without the peer multiple the card asks for (CMNP 8.98x, IPCC 4.31x).

conservatism_audit.note: Understated: terminal growth 2.0% against the model's own stated 3% nominal and deck CPI 3.28%, worth roughly 800 per share; terminal capex held at 19% of revenue, about 1.3x D&A, for twenty years. Overstated the other way: tax at 14.0% for twenty years against 24.3% actually paid in FY2025, and FY2026E profit 15.6% above the only sourced full-year guidance, with the scenario shocks hitting two drivers and neither of the named capex ones.

calibration.note: The engine's margin gate passes honestly (49.2% FY2026E against 50.4% blended on 9M2026 actual), but the year is not calibrated to S8's 'flat, not down' guidance: FY2026E NP of 4,232 needs Q4 of 1,582, +79% on the 9M run-rate, in the quarter management describes as merely Nataru-assisted.

signoff.notes: Batch check across TOLL_ROADS: all three names are BUY, so I looked for a shared cause before approving. None in the arithmetic: the sector trades at low trailing multiples (P/E 5.4x, P/B 0.51x, EV/EBITDA 8.0x on our FY2026E) against DCF values, and the shared reason is that the market prices these leveraged, build-cycle, state-linked assets as rate-sensitive in a CAUTIOUS balance-of-payments regime; each report holds the BI rate rather than needing cuts (this one keeps 6.0pc cash cost of debt and a 16.1pc COE, the highest in the batch). JSMR is the widest outlier at +159.5pc and the report supplies the reason: the reverse DCF shows the price implies FY2027E revenue growth of 0.74pc against 2.10pc in the base, a permanent stall below the operating revenue delivered in 9M2026, plus a sourced capex step-down after Gending-Paiton opened in October 2026. No identical inputs across names (growth -1.9/+5.5/+8.0pc, gross margin 43.7/19.5/72.5pc, tax 20/22/26.5pc). The target chain reproduces: blend 4,907 rolled to 5,542, scenario-weighted 6,902, and the report discloses that the bull carries more than half of it. All 15 FATAL and MATERIAL challenges are answered on substance and the AFFO gate is computed rather than substituted. Residual QC items Q9-Q12 are text or placeholder defects, not valuation: the market capitalisation in the AFFO paragraph prints as IDR19,741,409,664.00tn (six orders out), section 5 prints scenario weights 0.2/0.2 against a 0.25/0.25 model, one capex sentence mixes FY2026E with FY2029E, and params_basis says twenty-year against horizon 35. Route these to the renderer; none moves the rating. For the Director: the EV/EBITDA cross-check uses the own four-year mean of 13.7x against a peer median of 4.31x, disclosed and at only 30pc weight, but the one input I would revisit next session.

bias.note: Base FY2026E EBITDA margin 49.2% sits below the 9M2026 actual 50.4% (10,500/20,820) and revenue -1.9% is in line with 9M -1.2%; the +4.7pp lift vs FY2025A 44.5% is sourced construction-mix [S8][S15], not operating leverage. Conservative offsets: WACC prices debt at 9.45% vs 6.0% cash cost, terminal growth 3.0% vs deck CPI 3.28%. Optimistic offsets: tax 20% vs 24.3% FY2025 actual [S0], and the 25% bull (four mirrored shocks) is 53% of the target, disclosed in s5; the base alone is +104% and the bear Rp1,775 is below the Rp2,720 price. findings.finding: Investment summary reverses the two return metrics: it prints 159.5pct (val.tr_pct, which includes the Rp156 DPS) as 'above the Rp2,720 price' and 153.7pct (val.upside_pct, price-only) as 'a return'. fund record tr_pct=159.48, upside_pct=153.74, so the headline understates price upside and mislabels total return.

s3 and s6 state the FY2025 dividend as '1,100 IDR bn, or 31.0pct of net profit, equivalent to 156.2 per share'. 1,100/7,257.87m shares is 151.6 per share (5.6pct yield), while 156.2 is 31.0pct of np_parent 3,659.5, i.e. Rp1,134bn, which is the model dps [S0][S4]. The amount, payout and per-share cannot all hold as printed.

Q12 is only half cleared: params.horizon is 35 (FY2026E-FY2060E) and params_basis now says so, but the terminal_growth basis still reads 'The 20-year horizon and the dcf_life cut keep the terminal value from capitalising an expiring concession'. The horizon is 35 years and dcf_fcff does carry a terminal value of 12.1pct of its EV, so the sentence is stale on both counts.

s3 says core profit was 2,740bn, 'higher year on year [S18]', but facts F36 (S19) carries 9M2025 core profit also at 2,740bn, so the report's own table shows it flat; S18's +5.02pct implies about 2,609. The two archived sources conflict and the prose asserts the favourable reading without flagging it.

The EV/EBITDA cross-check still shows own history (13.66x) only, against the method card's 'vs peers and own history'. The pack peer median is 4.31x (CMNP 8.98, IPCC 4.31, IPCM 3.32, KARW 2.20, PORT 9.21) and JSMR trades at 11.6x current EV over the same pack LTM EBITDA, so the omission is not neutral to a reader of the 30pct weight. Q13 remains open.

s4 lists rf 7.4pct, ERP 4.2pct, CRP 2.5pct and levered beta 1.54 and prints COE 16.1pct, but those inputs imply about 16.4pct; the engine's 16.106pct comes from rf 7.45pct minus a 1.62pct default spread plus 1.536x(4.23+2.46)pct. The default-spread deduction is not disclosed.
s6 says 'insiders hold 74.3pct and institutions 17.4pct, leaving a free float of 24.6pct', which sums to 116.3pct as written; institutions sit inside the 24.6pct float (Q17 unchanged).

s5 describes a 13 November 2026 corporate-action and 2027-target release (including a buyback plan) as unarchived, but valuation.post_bs_review records only the earlier buyback-under-study sources [S9][S10] and does not log the 13 November event or its status; the KB carries the release as material news. Q16 remains open.

flags.message: a.gross_margin moves +10.8pp from FY2026E to FY2060E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: The blended margin rises only because zero-margin construction revenue contracts 21.41% yoy to Rp5.15tn of 9M2026 revenue [S8][S15], while the toll operating margin is held at the disclosed 67.0% EBITDA margin [S3]. The lift is mix arithmetic on sourced segment revenue, not an assumed operating improvement, and the terminal 54.5% still sits below the 67.0% toll-only margin.

flags.message: a.capex_pct moves -21.9pp from FY2026E to FY2060E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: Capex falls from the 43.8% build peak as construction revenue contracts 21.41% [S8] and the Gending-Paiton section, the last of the current Trans-Java programme, opened in October 2026 [S2]. Yogyakarta-Bawen is funded by its own Rp17.92tn syndicated facility [S5]; the 19.0% floor still funds widening and resurfacing, so the drift is a sourced end of the build cycle, not a maintenance holiday.

flags.message: expected return +159%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The return comes from three sourced drivers: construction revenue contracting 21.41% yoy to Rp5.15tn of 9M2026 revenue removes the zero-margin pass-through [S8]; capex normalises after Gending-Paiton opened in October 2026 and Yogyakarta-Bawen carries its own Rp17.92tn facility [S2][S5]; and ten sections enter their biennial tariff reset in 2026 [S14]. The reverse-DCF solver puts the Rp2,720 price at FY2027E revenue growth of 0.74% against 2.10% in our base (dcf_fcff method), so the price pays for a permanent stall in revenue growth rather than for a higher discount rate; 9M2026 operating revenue still grew 7.9% [S2], which is what the rating rests on, and the bear case is disclosed as below the price rather than as a floor.

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'dcf_fcff': 0.6, 'ev_ebitda': 0.25, 'pbv': 0.15}
flags.justification: House TOLL_ROADS defaults are dcf_fcff 0.6 / ev_ebitda 0.25 / pbv 0.15 [config]. We move the DCF to the concession-life form (dcf_life) so no perpetuity is capitalised on reverting concessions, and we drop P/BV to zero rather than keep a token 5%: on parent book equity the shares are above book, so the multiple is not a discount anchor for this name and a weighted method that cannot inform the decision is worse than none [S0][S6]. EV/EBITDA takes the freed weight as the market cross-check, computed on the data pack's own LTM EBITDA series and the pack's own-history multiple: the multiple and the metric must come from the same series, because the pack understates EBITDA through its D&A line, so the cross-check is never applied to the restated disclosed series [S0][S3].
